questions.audio_text: People often say that wheels make moving a load easier because they reduce friction. That's useful as a starting point, but it can lead to a mistaken goal: removing friction everywhere. Let's look at a cart. Resistance inside a poorly working wheel bearing makes the wheel harder to turn. Reducing that resistance can help the cart move more easily. At the point where a driven wheel meets the ground, however, grip matters. Without enough friction there, the wheel can spin without moving the cart forward as intended. Brakes give us another example: friction can be used deliberately to slow motion. So the design question isn't simply, how do we get rid of friction? It's, where is friction helping, and where is it wasting effort? The same cart contains different contact surfaces with different jobs. A change that helps one part move smoothly may be unsuitable for a surface that needs to grip. We have to describe the location and purpose before judging friction as good or bad.

questions.prompt: What is the talk mainly exploring?
options: Why one model fits all plants.
Why more leaves guarantee uniform light.

questions.audio_text: Look down on a plant from above. Some leaves overlap, so an upper leaf may shade one below it. The total area of all the leaves therefore isn't the same as the area that receives direct light at one moment. Their arrangement matters too. We can explore that with a simple model. Put several identical paper leaves on a vertical support under a lamp. First place them directly above one another. Then turn some around the support, keeping the same number, size, and height of leaves. More of the lower paper surfaces may now receive direct light. This model illustrates how changing positions can reduce overlap. It doesn't establish one perfect arrangement for every real plant. Sunlight comes from different directions during the day, nearby plants cast shadows, and real leaves differ in shape and angle. Also, paper doesn't grow or use energy, so this is a model of light exposure, not a complete model of plant growth. If we compare arrangements, we should describe the lighting and leaf shapes we used. Otherwise a result from one setup might be mistaken for a universal rule.

questions.audio_text: Before you draw that bicycle, look at the spaces inside its frame. You'll see shapes bounded by the metal tubes. In drawing, we can pay attention to these spaces as well as to the solid object. They're examples of negative space: the area around or between the forms we're focusing on. Negative doesn't mean bad or unimportant. Here's a useful exercise. Instead of drawing what you remember a bicycle looks like, copy the shapes of those gaps. Their edges also establish the edges of the tubes. If one gap is too wide in your drawing, you have a clue that the surrounding parts need adjusting. You don't have to leave every gap white; the term describes its relationship to the subject, not a required color. Shifting attention in this way can help you check proportions without getting caught up in naming every part of the bicycle.

questions.prompt: What does the speaker explain about musical variation?
questions.passage_title: Recognizing a musical idea after it changes
options: It mainly depends on adding more notes to a melody.
It combines a recognizable connection with a change.
It requires different instruments to play identical pitches.
It replaces each short musical idea with a complete new song.
questions.audio_text: A composer doesn't always need a new melody to make something interesting happen. Sometimes a short musical idea, called a motif, returns in a changed form. Imagine a three-note figure with a clear pattern: two short notes followed by a longer one. Later, a different instrument plays that same rhythmic pattern, but on different pitches. You may hear a connection even though it isn't an exact copy. That's the useful tension in variation: something stays recognizable while something else changes. Now, not every group of three notes belongs to the same motif. We need to listen for the particular relationships that made the first figure distinctive. In our example, rhythm supplies that link. In another piece, the rise and fall of the notes might matter more. When you describe a variation, name both sides of the comparison. What has been retained? What has been altered? Saying only that the music repeats misses the composer's work with change.

questions.prompt: What is the talk mainly about?
questions.passage_title: When a performer speaks to the audience
options: Why spectators should avoid speaking during a performance.
How direct address gives theater audiences a role in a scene.
How actors recover when they forget a character's lines.

questions.audio_text: Imagine a stage scene in which two characters argue about a missing letter. One character turns toward the audience and says, 'You saw where I put it, didn't you?' For a moment, the spectators aren't merely watching other people talk. They're being addressed. This technique, direct address, changes the relationship between the performance and the people watching it. A production can use it to invite agreement, share a secret, or question the audience's judgment. It needn't require a spoken reply. The actor might pause briefly and then continue the scene. Nor does the technique have one fixed emotional effect. A friendly appeal can make spectators feel included, while an accusation can make them uncomfortable. So when we analyze direct address, identifying the turn toward the audience is only a beginning. We also ask what role the words offer the spectators: witness, supporter, judge, or perhaps someone being challenged.

questions.prompt: What use of montage is illustrated in the talk?
questions.passage_title: A month of practice in a few shots
options: Replacing visual evidence with a spoken explanation.
Compressing a long process into selected moments.
Showing several camera angles of the same brief action.
Recording a repair in one continuous unedited shot.
questions.audio_text: Let's say we're making a short film about someone learning to repair a violin. We could show every practice session, but that would take hours. Instead, we choose a few shots: a hand slipping, a pile of rejected pieces, a calendar with later dates, and finally a repair that holds. Arranged together, these selected moments can suggest a longer period of effort. This is one use of a montage sequence. Notice that the viewer does some connecting work. No single shot says that a month of improvement has passed; the sequence supplies the relationship. Order matters, too. Put the successful repair first and the failures afterward, and viewers may think the learner is losing confidence or skill. Music can support the sequence, but it isn't what defines it. For our classroom exercise, we'll try the same set of shots in two orders without a soundtrack, then discuss how the implied story changes.

Why poster deadlines should be expressed as specific times.

questions.audio_text: In this design exercise, the words on a poster will stay the same. What we'll change is where each line ends. Suppose the poster says, 'Please return borrowed tools before Friday.' If 'before Friday' remains together, readers can take in the deadline as a unit. Separating 'before' from 'Friday' puts the relationship across two lines, which may be less convenient in a quick glance. A line break can also give a phrase visual emphasis simply by placing it on its own. That doesn't mean every phrase deserves a separate line. Too many breaks can make readers assemble a sentence from scattered pieces. We're balancing groups of meaning, available width, and emphasis. Start by reading the sentence aloud in natural groups. Then try a layout that respects those groups, and check it at the distance from which the poster will actually be read.

questions.prompt: What does the talk mainly explain?
questions.passage_title: New ocean floor at a spreading ridge
options: How older oceanic crust melts as it approaches the center of a ridge.
Why mountains under the ocean stop the movement of tectonic plates.
How oceanic crust forms at a ridge and records its movement away.
Why ridges producing the youngest rocks have the fastest present motion.
questions.audio_text: You might picture the ocean floor as a fixed surface under the water. Near a mid-ocean ridge, though, new ocean floor is being made. A ridge is a long underwater mountain system. Here, two tectonic plates, large moving pieces of Earth's outer layer, pull apart. Molten rock rises into the opening, cools, and becomes new oceanic crust. As more crust forms, earlier crust moves away on either side. How could we check that picture without watching for millions of years? We can determine the ages of rocks at different distances from a ridge. Generally, the youngest rocks are near the center, and older rocks lie farther away. That age pattern fits crust forming at the ridge and then traveling outward. The rocks' ages can also help us compare spreading rates. Suppose we locate rocks of the same age beside two different ridges. If they've traveled farther from one ridge, the crust there has moved away faster on average over that time. Keep the time period the same when making that comparison. And remember, an average over a million years doesn't tell us the speed at this exact moment; the rate may have changed. So the seafloor preserves a record of both its formation and its later movement.

It pushes the two plates together and closes the opening.

options: On average, crust moved away faster at Ridge Y during that period.
On average, crust moved away faster at Ridge X during that period.
The crust moved at the same average rate because the rocks have the same age.
Crust at Ridge Y is moving twice as fast as crust at Ridge X at this moment.
questions.audio_text: You might picture the ocean floor as a fixed surface under the water. Near a mid-ocean ridge, though, new ocean floor is being made. A ridge is a long underwater mountain system. Here, two tectonic plates, large moving pieces of Earth's outer layer, pull apart. Molten rock rises into the opening, cools, and becomes new oceanic crust. As more crust forms, earlier crust moves away on either side. How could we check that picture without watching for millions of years? We can determine the ages of rocks at different distances from a ridge. Generally, the youngest rocks are near the center, and older rocks lie farther away. That age pattern fits crust forming at the ridge and then traveling outward. The rocks' ages can also help us compare spreading rates. Suppose we locate rocks of the same age beside two different ridges. If they've traveled farther from one ridge, the crust there has moved away faster on average over that time. Keep the time period the same when making that comparison. And remember, an average over a million years doesn't tell us the speed at this exact moment; the rate may have changed. So the seafloor preserves a record of both its formation and its later movement.

questions.prompt: What is the talk mainly explaining?
questions.passage_title: What the date on a buried coin can establish
options: How the value of a coin determines how long it remains in circulation.
How a coin can set a limit on a deposit's date without giving its exact age.
Why archaeologists generally prefer old coins to recently produced ones.
Why sealed deposits rarely contain objects from different years.
questions.audio_text: Here's a dating problem from an imaginary excavation. A sealed deposit contains a coin that we know was made in 1720. For this example, we've checked that the coin belongs to the deposit and wasn't pushed into it by later disturbance. Could the deposit have been sealed in 1700? No, because that coin didn't exist yet. Its production date gives us an earliest possible date for sealing the deposit: 1720. But don't replace 'earliest possible' with 'exact.' Coins can remain in use, be saved, or be passed down. This one might have entered the deposit many years after it was made. Imagine it was kept in a family for sixty years before burial. Its production and burial dates would then be quite far apart. If another securely associated coin was produced in 1740, that later object would move our earliest possible date forward to 1740. Adding older coins would not move it backward. This logic depends on the association we checked at the start. A later object that slipped through a crack into an older deposit would not date the original sealing event. So we need two kinds of care: identifying when an object could first have existed, and establishing how it relates to the event we're trying to date. A date on an object answers a narrower question than beginners sometimes expect.

questions.prompt: What challenge in adaptive reuse does the talk emphasize?
questions.passage_title: Giving an old building a new job
options: Preserving each room by preventing it from being used again.
Choosing the new activity solely according to the building's age.
Meeting a new purpose while respecting meaningful existing features.
Making a building look as though its new function were its original one.
questions.audio_text: Suppose a town has an empty fire station and needs a small community library. One option is adaptive reuse: giving an existing building a new purpose. This doesn't mean pretending the fire station was always a library. Its wide vehicle doors might remain visible even if reading areas are built behind them. The design has to serve present users while considering the features that tell the building's story. Some changes will be practical necessities, such as making the entrance accessible or providing suitable lighting. Others may be avoidable. Imagine covering all the old brickwork just to make every room look identical. Before doing that, designers should ask what would be lost and whether the new use really requires it. Reuse isn't automatically suitable for every building or every proposed activity. A noisy workshop and a quiet reading room have different needs. The useful question is whether the building's existing qualities and the intended use can be made to work together.

questions.prompt: What is the main focus of the talk?
options: Why formal reports should copy everyday conversations.
The best technical terms for describing computer failures.
Language choices that change with setting and purpose.
How regional dialects disappear when speakers attend college.
questions.audio_text: Think about a student explaining the same broken computer to two people. To a roommate, she might say, 'It keeps freezing.' In a technical report, she might describe when the system stops responding and use more specialized terms. The speaker and the problem are the same, but the situation and purpose have changed. We can discuss that adjustment in terms of register. Register includes choices associated with an activity or setting, including how formal or technical the language is. Now compare that with dialect, which involves patterns associated with a region or social group. These aren't two names for the same distinction. A person may shift into a formal register while retaining features of a regional dialect. And casual language isn't necessarily careless language. A short expression may work very well between people who share background knowledge. The question is how language choices fit the audience and the task, not whether one speaker is generally better than another.

questions.prompt: What does the talk explain?
questions.passage_title: A question that asks someone to act
options: How a question's purpose can differ from its grammatical form.
Why questions about ability are unsuitable in ordinary conversation.
Why requests must contain a direct command to be understood.
How doctors can avoid asking patients to perform movements.
questions.audio_text: If I say, 'Could you move that bag?' I'm probably not conducting a study of your physical abilities. In an ordinary conversation, you would usually understand a request to move it. The sentence has the form of a question about ability, but its social purpose is to get an action done. That's one way requests can be indirect. Context does important work here. Imagine instead that a doctor asks the same question during a test of an injured arm. Now information about ability could be exactly what is wanted. So we shouldn't attach one intention permanently to the words. We consider the activity, the relationship between the speakers, and what happens next. If someone responds, 'Sure,' and moves the bag, both people have treated the question as a request. If the answer describes pain and limited movement during the examination, the same grammatical form is doing a different job.

questions.prompt: What does the speaker explain about sentence stress?
questions.passage_title: Emphasizing a different part of a sentence
options: It allows listeners to identify every unspoken detail with certainty.
It replaces the need to consider the words around an emphasized word.
It can change the focus without changing the basic event described.
It normally changes a statement into a question about a different event.
questions.audio_text: Let's use one sentence: 'Maya borrowed the red notebook.' We can keep all the words and still shift the focus by stressing a different word. If we put extra emphasis on Maya, we may be correcting someone who thought Leo borrowed it. If we emphasize red, we may be distinguishing that notebook from a blue one. Notice that the basic event hasn't changed: Maya borrowed a notebook. What changes is the contrast we're inviting the listener to consider. Stress can guide attention toward information that is new, disputed, or especially relevant. But it doesn't spell out every alternative by itself. A strong emphasis on red won't tell us whether the other color was blue, green, or something else unless the context supplies that detail. When interpreting emphasis, connect the highlighted word to the conversation around it rather than inventing a complete missing story.

questions.prompt: What is the talk mainly about?
questions.passage_title: Following a metaphor through several sentences
options: Why each sentence in an explanation needs a new unrelated comparison.
Why research reports should replace technical information with stories.
How a continuing metaphor can organize an explanation and still have limits.
How travelers can choose a route when they reach a physical dead end.
questions.audio_text: A metaphor can do more than decorate one sentence. A speaker may carry the same comparison through a whole explanation. Imagine a teacher describing a research project as a journey. She might speak of choosing a route, reaching a dead end, and going back to an earlier turning point. The project hasn't literally moved down a road. The travel language organizes relationships among decisions, obstacles, and revisions. Because the comparison continues, one phrase can prepare us to understand the next. Now there's a limit. If the teacher says the project needs more fuel, listeners have to decide what fuel stands for here: perhaps time, money, or effort. The comparison alone doesn't settle that. A useful extended metaphor makes selected relationships easier to follow, but it shouldn't replace a clear explanation of the actual project. When you analyze one, ask which features of the familiar situation are being carried over and which would be misleading if taken literally.

questions.prompt: What difficulty with homophones does the talk describe?
questions.passage_title: When the sound does not choose the spelling

questions.audio_text: Consider the words meaning 'a pair of shoes' and 'a pear to eat.' The first is spelled p, a, i, r; the fruit is spelled p, e, a, r. For many English speakers, they sound the same, although their spellings and meanings differ. Words like these are called homophones. Context usually helps. If a sentence is about putting on shoes, the two-item meaning fits; if it is about slicing fruit, the fruit meaning fits. This is why simply reading your sentence aloud may fail to reveal a homophone error. The wrong written word can still sound perfectly acceptable. During revision, look at the meaning each spelling represents and ask whether it fits the sentence. Check written meaning, not just sound.

questions.prompt: What choice in writing does the talk explore?
questions.passage_title: How close a narrator feels to a character

questions.audio_text: Let's describe one moment in two ways. First: 'A woman waited outside the office.' Now: 'Lena pressed her damp palms together. Why hadn't anyone called her name?' The second version brings us closer to a particular character's physical sensations and immediate concerns. We can discuss this as a change in narrative distance. Distance here isn't measured in meters. It's about how closely the narration engages us with a character's experience. A more distant account can summarize a long period or describe several people efficiently. A closer account can slow a brief moment and direct attention to what it feels like. Neither choice is automatically superior. A writer may begin with a broad view of a busy office and then move closer to one person as her situation becomes central. When revising, ask what the reader needs at that point: a wider overview, an intimate experience, or a controlled movement between the two.

questions.prompt: What is the main purpose of the talk?
questions.passage_title: Two kinds of cost at a badge booth
options: To distinguish costs by how they respond to output.
To recommend a particular price for selling badges.
To compare the quality of two badge-making machines.
To explain why renting equipment prevents a profit.
questions.audio_text: Let's put ourselves in charge of a badge booth for one afternoon. We rent a small machine for sixty dollars. That charge covers the afternoon whether we make ten badges or a hundred, so we'll call it a fixed cost for this activity. The plain badge pieces are different. Each piece costs one dollar, and every badge we make uses another piece. That is a variable cost: it changes with the number produced. Now, if we double production, do our total costs double? Not in this simple example. The materials bill doubles, but the machine charge stays the same. The rental cost spread across each badge becomes smaller. Notice that I said 'for this activity.' If we add a second afternoon, we need another rental period. A cost can be fixed within a particular plan without being fixed forever. Before comparing two production plans, then, ask what time period and what amount of output each plan includes. Otherwise, we might call the same charge fixed in one sentence and variable in the next without explaining why.

questions.audio_text: Imagine that a shop owner pays a gardener to plant flowers beside the entrance. The owner enjoys the display and hopes customers will enjoy it too. But people walking past on the public path also enjoy the flowers, even if they never enter the shop. In economics, that last benefit is a positive external effect: someone outside the purchase receives a benefit. The owner's pleasure is a private benefit, so we keep the two categories separate. Now, suppose the owner is deciding whether to pay for another flower bed. The owner might compare the price with benefits to the shop, leaving the pleasure of passing strangers out of the calculation. The display could therefore be worth more to everyone together than to the person paying for it. That doesn't tell us the exact size of either benefit. It tells us what a calculation limited to the buyer can miss. If neighbors offered to help pay because they valued the view, that would change the owner's comparison without changing the gardener's price.

questions.prompt: What is the talk mainly explaining?
questions.passage_title: A coin does not owe us a different result
options: How a coin gradually repairs an uneven record of results.
Why five heads is as likely as one head before tossing begins.
Why earlier results do not alter the next independent toss.
How to make a fair coin produce alternating heads and tails.
questions.audio_text: Let's use a simple probability model: a fair coin, with independent tosses. Fair means that heads and tails are equally likely on each toss. Independent means that knowing earlier results doesn't change the chances on the next toss. Suppose we have just seen four heads in a row. Someone says, 'Surely tails is due now.' That sounds like the coin needs to correct the record, but our model contains no such rule. The next toss still has equal chances of heads and tails. Now be careful about a different question. Before any tossing begins, predicting five heads in a row is a much more demanding prediction than predicting heads on just one toss. Once four heads have already occurred, however, only the fifth result remains uncertain. We must distinguish predicting a whole sequence in advance from predicting its final event after the earlier events are known. A surprising past sequence doesn't, by itself, make an independent future toss compensate for it.

questions.prompt: What is the main distinction in the talk?
questions.passage_title: Two percentages on an imaginary class report
options: Scores from a short quiz versus scores from a longer quiz.

questions.audio_text: Imagine that our statistics class invents a report with two numbers for a quiz. The first is percent correct: the share of questions a student answers correctly. The second describes the student's position compared with other students. For this exercise, we'll use a simple percentile-rank rule: compare one student with one hundred others, and report how many of those others scored lower. Assume there are no ties involving our student. This is a classroom illustration, not a scoring rule for a particular examination. Now, Maya answers sixty percent of the questions correctly, and eighty of the hundred comparison students score lower. Her two numbers are sixty and eighty. There is no contradiction. One compares correct answers with quiz questions; the other compares Maya with people. If we keep her answers unchanged but compare her with a stronger group, her relative position can fall while her percent correct stays at sixty. Conversely, answering more questions correctly doesn't guarantee a higher relative position if everyone else improves even more. So, when someone says a score is a percentage, ask: a percentage of what? Questions and people are different denominators. The number alone isn't enough to tell us what was measured. And to compare rankings fairly, we need to know which group supplied the comparison.

questions.prompt: What is the speaker's main point?
questions.passage_title: Two sales records and a third factor
options: Bicycle rentals provide a direct measure of campus temperature.
A shared factor may explain an observed association.
More rentals directly cause the entire observed rise in water sales.

questions.audio_text: Imagine a campus rental shop compares its bicycle rentals with bottled-water sales over a month. On days with more rentals, more water is sold too. It's tempting to draw an arrow from renting a bicycle to buying water. But we haven't yet earned that arrow. Consider the temperature. Warm weather could encourage more cycling and also make people want more water, including people who never rent a bicycle. Temperature would then be a third factor influencing both records. To explore that possibility, we could compare days with similar temperatures instead of mixing hot and cool days together. Suppose, in our imaginary data, the connection between the two sales figures becomes much weaker within those temperature groups. That would support the idea that temperature helps explain the original pattern. It wouldn't prove that cycling never makes anyone thirsty. We're considering what explains a pattern in these records, not denying every possible connection between the activities. Seeing two quantities rise together gives us a question to investigate; it doesn't automatically give us the causal answer.

questions.prompt: What is the main idea of the demonstration?
questions.passage_title: Making current by changing a magnetic field
options: A nearby magnet supplies a steady current while its distance from a coil stays fixed.
Moving a magnet is necessary because turning a coil does not change the electrical effect.
A change in how much magnetic field passes through a coil can produce a current in a closed circuit.
A coil stores the current from a moving magnet and releases it after the magnet stops.
questions.audio_text: Here's a coil, a length of wire wound into loops, connected to a sensitive meter in a closed circuit. I'll move a bar magnet toward the opening of the coil. See the meter's needle move? That indicates a current. Now I'll hold the magnet still. The needle returns to zero, even though the magnet is still close to the wire. When I pull the magnet away, the needle moves in the opposite direction, indicating a reversed current. What matters is a change in the amount of magnetic field passing through the coil, not simply having a magnet nearby. Producing an electrical effect this way is called electromagnetic induction. If I repeat the same movement faster, the needle makes a larger brief movement. But stopping the magnet again brings the reading back to zero. This principle also helps explain a generator. Imagine a handle that turns a coil between magnets. As the coil rotates, the amount of magnetic field passing through it keeps changing, and this can drive a current around a connected circuit. Notice that turning the handle takes effort. The generator converts the mechanical energy we supply into electrical energy. The magnet helps make the process possible; it isn't an endless supply of energy by itself.

questions.prompt: What does the proposed exercise compare?
questions.passage_title: Equal practice time arranged on different days
options: Reading symbols aloud versus copying them silently.
Learning on weekdays versus learning only during vacations.
Different symbol sets studied for different amounts of time.
Different distributions of equal practice time.
questions.audio_text: We're going to design a classroom exercise about practice schedules. Imagine two groups learning the same set of unfamiliar symbols. One group practices for thirty minutes on Friday. The other practices for ten minutes on Monday, ten on Wednesday, and ten on Friday. Their total practice time is equal, but its distribution is different. Both groups take a test the following Friday. Why wait? A test immediately after practice tells us about performance at that moment. We're interested in what remains after a delay. Now, suppose the spread-out group remembers more symbols on the delayed test. That would favor its schedule in this exercise, provided the groups and their materials were otherwise comparable. It wouldn't show that adding breaks is best for every task or every possible delay. We should also record how well each group did at the end of practice. If we record only one time point, we may confuse easy performance during practice with lasting retention. The comparison needs a clear schedule, equal total practice, and a stated time for measuring the result.

questions.prompt: What principle is the speaker illustrating?
options: Nearby elements tend to be perceived as a group.
A border is required for people to perceive separate groups.
Identical buttons must perform the same function.
Text labels are understood independently of their location.
questions.audio_text: Look at the imagined arrangement I'm describing: six identical buttons in one horizontal row. There is a small gap between the first three, a much wider gap, and then three more with small gaps between them. You probably picture two groups. I haven't changed the buttons' colors or added a border; I've changed their spacing. This illustrates grouping by proximity, the tendency to see nearby elements as belonging together. Designers can use it when laying out controls. For example, a label placed close to one group of buttons may seem to describe that group. But proximity is a cue, not a guarantee that the items really have the same function. If the label actually belongs to a more distant group, the spacing can mislead. The designer should bring the intended relationship and the visual relationship into agreement. Before adding another box or heading, it can be useful to ask whether the gaps are already suggesting the right groups.

questions.prompt: What is the main lesson from the two rounds?
questions.passage_title: A faster answer with more mistakes
options: Performance should be evaluated using both speed and accuracy.
One average response time fully captures both speed and errors.
The quickest response always indicates the most skilled participant.
Changing instructions prevents any meaningful comparison of a task.
questions.audio_text: Imagine a simple laboratory task. A shape appears on a screen, and a participant presses one key for a circle and another for a square. In one round, the instruction emphasizes accuracy. In another, it emphasizes answering quickly. Suppose the participant responds faster in the second round but makes more mistakes. We shouldn't describe that as an improvement in speed and stop there. The result shows a trade-off: gaining speed came with a loss of accuracy in this example. To compare performance, we need both the response times and the error rates. We also need to know what the task values. A practice game might reward quick responses, whereas checking a sensitive record might place a much greater cost on an error. Does this mean people can never become both faster and more accurate? No. Practice or a clearer display might improve both. Our example concerns a change in how one participant balances competing demands, not a permanent limit on what that person can learn.
